newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Opposition wins big, also claims big fraud.
newsitem.headline: Opposition wins big, also claims big fraud.

text.p: Opposition coalition Zajedno dealt a stunning blow to the prestige of President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialists by winning control over Serbia's biggest cities, including the capital Belgrade.

"Zajedno won 60 seats, the Socialist Party of Serbia 23, the Serbian Radical Party 15 and the Serbian Democratic Party won two," Belgrade election commission chairman Dragoslav Lazarevic told reporters on Tuesday.
Lazarevic said that in Belgrade voting would be repeated for 10 counsellors. The city assembly has 110 seats.
Celebrating Belgraders, many with tears in their eyes, claimed a new era of democracy was dawning over Serbia as a result of Sunday's municipal elections.
But this was not in evidence elsewhere as tensions rose when thousands of opposition supporters protested against what they called massive fraud engineered to deny them victory.
Socialist-controlled election commissions in several big towns annulled the results, claiming voting irregularities, and called for a third round of polls for November 27.

"This is unprecedented violence over the voters wishes. The authorities have commited countless criminal acts of forgery," said Zoran Djindjic, the leader of the Democratic Party, a Zajedno coalition partner.

"The Socialists simply cannot admit their defeat and are trying to provoke disturbances and demonstrations throughout the country," he said. "The world cannot turn a blind eye to this flagrant disrespect for the law."
Such allegations could embarass Milosevic already under harsh scrutiny by the United States.
Washington has retained an outter wall of sanctions against Belgrade barring it from desperately needed foreign capital. until it improves its human rights record.
The United States embassy in Belgrade gave a clean bill of health to the federal elections two weeks ago but warned the polls were just a part of evolving democratic process.
"Human rights and freedoms are in the forefront of U.S. policy towards Serbia," U.S. envoy John Kornblum recently said.

The authorities were putting up a bitter fight in the Serbian industrial town of Nis, where thousands protested the city's commission decision to annul results from as many as 19 polling stations stripping the opposition of a clean victory.
Opposition leaders have promised not to budge from the city hall until the commission revokes its decision.
A bakery belonging to a socialist official in Nis was demolished, prompting fears of police retaliation.
Results were also cancelled in the towns of Smederevska Palanka, Jagodina, Pancevo and Uzice. Protests spilled over into the streets and some leaders staged hunger strikes.
The election commission in Novi Sad, the provincial capital of Vojvodina, promised results on Wednesday in a clear violation of the law which stipulates them by Tuesday evening,
The opposition also claimed victory in Kragujevac, Uzice, Kraljevo, Kikinda, Zrenjanin, Cacak and Novi Sad.
The scale of the Socialists' defeat could only be explained by complacency into which they were lulled by their victory at federal elections two weeks ago.

The loss of the major cities, where industrial unrest against poverty and joblessness has recently increased, would be a severe blow to the Socialists' prestige ahead of Serbian parliamentary elections scheduled for next year.
The socialists maintain a tight grip over electronic media which enabled them easy election victories so far.
But opposition leader Vuk Draskovic promised to relax that grip quickly once the new city government takes over.
